design_detail: Controlled cross-sectional inpatient study at a clinical research centre (Johns Hopkins, Baltimore). 30 people who had used MDMA on at least 25 occasions and 28 controls who had never used it were admitted after at least 2 weeks of agreed abstinence and kept on a low-monoamine diet. Outcomes: lumbar CSF monoamine metabolites (5-HIAA, HVA, MHPG) on the third morning; prolactin response to intravenous L-tryptophan; ischaemic pain by the tourniquet test; personality questionnaires (Multidimensional Personality Questionnaire, Buss-Durkee Hostility Inventory, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire). No tests of memory or thinking.
can_establish: That this self-referred group of people who had used MDMA many times had lower lumbar CSF 5-HIAA than this control group under standardized inpatient conditions, and whether neuroendocrine, pain and personality measures differed between the two groups.
cannot_establish: That MDMA caused the lower 5-HIAA (no pre-use measure, and much heavier use of other drugs in the MDMA group that was not adjusted for); that the lower metabolite level reflects loss of serotonin nerve terminals rather than lower serotonin turnover (the authors write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from CSF data alone, p. 135); any effect on memory or thinking (none was measured); or how much use matters (5-HIAA was not related to any measure of use).

sample.recruitment: MDMA group self-referred: they telephoned one of the investigators after learning of ongoing MDMA research at the Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions. Controls were referred by people in the MDMA group or recruited from the Baltimore/Washington area. Telephone screen, then medical, neurological and psychiatric screening on admission (Methods › Subjects, p. 130).
sample.inclusion_exclusion: MDMA group: good health and MDMA used on at least 25 occasions; earlier use of other drugs allowed. Controls: the same health criteria and no MDMA exposure. Both groups excluded for past or present major medical illness, pregnancy, HIV seropositivity, history of psychosis, current major depressive disorder and current alcohol or drug dependence (p. 130).
sample.demographics: Controls: mean age 27.8 (SD 7.8), education 16.5 (2.8) years; MDMA group: 32.3 (13.6) and 15.2 (2.0). Men in the MDMA group had less education than control men, 14.8 (1.6) vs 17.2 (2.6) years, marked significant (Table 1, p. 131; group x gender interaction F(1, 53) = 4.4, p = .04, p. 132). The text states that there were no significant socioeconomic, ethnic, racial or occupational differences, without data (Results › Demographics, p. 132).
sample.attrition: Not applicable (single admission). The prolactin analysis includes 51 of the 58 participants (control women 7 of 11, control men 16 of 17, MDMA women 10 of 12), with no explanation (Table 5, p. 133).
sample.selection_effects: The MDMA group selected itself by contacting an MDMA research programme, and the authors describe its members as often strong advocates of the drug's benefits (p. 136); some controls were referred by them. Lifetime use of other drugs was far more common in the MDMA group (cocaine 80% vs 29%, LSD and other hallucinogens 87% vs 32%, benzodiazepines 60% vs 21%; Table 3, p. 131). Exclusion of current depression, psychosis and dependence makes both groups healthier than many people who use MDMA.

exposure.measurement: Self-report only: a telephone interview, an MDMA questionnaire (number of occasions, usual amount, frequency, last use, highest amount), a standardized drug-history questionnaire and the Structured Clinical Interview for DSM-III-R (p. 130). Urine and blood drug screens were taken on arrival; their results are not reported. Tablet content was not tested.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Self-reported (Table 2, p. 131): 94.4 (SD 90.6) occasions, range 25 to 300; duration 4.98 (2.96) years, range 0.5 to 16; frequency 4.16 (4.79) times a month, range 0.15 to 20; time since last use 17.9 (24.7) weeks, range 2 to 104. The usual amount per occasion is misprinted and cannot be read (see reporting issues). Route not reported.
exposure.polysubstance: Allowed, and described only as any lifetime exposure by drug class (Table 3, p. 131), MDMA group vs controls: non-MDMA amphetamines 43% vs 14%, cocaine 80% vs 29%, benzodiazepines 60% vs 21%, sedative-hypnotics 33% vs 4%, LSD and other hallucinogens 87% vs 32%, cannabis 93% vs 73% as printed (22 of 28 is 79%), solvents 27% vs 29%, opiates 53% vs 32%, PCP 13% vs 7%. Frequency and recency of other drug use, alcohol and tobacco are not reported, and no analysis adjusts for other drug use. The authors argue that other drugs are unlikely to explain the CSF finding because controls also used them, to a lesser extent, and few drugs outside the amphetamine class are selectively neurotoxic (p. 136).
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: At least 2 weeks of agreed abstinence from all recreational drugs, with urine and blood screens on arrival (results not reported); time since last MDMA use 17.9 (24.7) weeks, range 2 to 104 (Table 2, p. 131). Lumbar puncture between 8 and 10 AM on the third morning of the stay, after an overnight fast and bed rest (p. 130).

comparison.controls: 28 healthy volunteers with no MDMA exposure, referred by MDMA participants or recruited locally; other recreational drug use allowed (p. 130).
comparison.matching: The Results call the groups well matched for age, height, weight and sex ratio (p. 132) and the Discussion calls the controls matched also for education and other drug use (p. 135); Table 1 shows less education in MDMA men and Table 3 more lifetime use of most other drug classes in the MDMA group. CSF analyses were adjusted for age and height only.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: No measure before MDMA use of CSF metabolites, personality or cognition. The authors argue against a premorbid explanation because people with psychiatric disorders involving serotonin were screened out and the groups did not differ on standardized psychiatric measures (p. 136); those psychiatric data are not shown.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Yes: cannabis 22 of 28 (printed 73%), LSD and other hallucinogens 32%, opiates 32%, cocaine 29%, solvents 29%, benzodiazepines 21% (Table 3, p. 131).

outcomes.instruments: CSF 5-HIAA, HVA and MHPG by high-performance liquid chromatography with electrochemical detection; control and MDMA samples processed and assayed together without knowledge of group (p. 130); intra- and inter-assay coefficients of variation 2.3% and 4.7% for 5-HIAA (Table 4, p. 133). Prolactin before and after 7 g intravenous L-tryptophan (basal level, peak change, area under the curve) (pp. 130-131). Submaximum-effort tourniquet ischaemic pain: sensitivity, endurance, tolerance (p. 131). Multidimensional Personality Questionnaire, Buss-Durkee Hostility Inventory, Eysenck Personality Questionnaire (pp. 131-132).
outcomes.validity_norms: Control CSF values are said to lie within the ranges reported for controls in other studies (p. 132). The use of lumbar CSF 5-HIAA as a marker rests on monkey studies cited by the authors, which they say show that it detects, but underestimates, serotonin damage produced by MDMA (p. 130).
outcomes.operationalization: Neurotoxicity is inferred from lower CSF 5-HIAA and from the absence, in the MDMA group, of the usual negative correlation between height and CSF 5-HIAA (pp. 132, 135); no direct measure of serotonin nerve terminals. No cognitive outcome.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: Bonferroni multivariate intervals for the personality measures only; Duncan's multiple range test for post hoc comparisons (p. 132). No correction across the CSF, neuroendocrine, pain and personality families. 16 counts the outcomes named in the Results (3 metabolites, 3 prolactin measures, 3 pain measures, 4 MPQ scales, 1 hostility scale, 2 EPQ scales); the questionnaires have more subscales than are reported.
outcomes.assessor_blinding: CSF assays blind to group (p. 130). Not reported for the other measures; the personality measures are self-report.

analysis.effect_sizes: CSF 5-HIAA: controls 15.2 (SD 7.9; range 4.8 to 37.3) vs MDMA group 10.3 (3.1) ng/ml; one-way ANCOVA with age and height, F(1, 54) = 11.6, p = .001; 2 x 2 group x gender ANCOVA, group F(1, 52) = 14.9, p < .001, interaction F(1, 52) = 5.1, p < .03 (Results › 5-HIAA, 1st paragraph, p. 132; Table 4, p. 133). Women 18.7 (9.3) vs 10.1 (2.6), 46% lower; men 13.4 (5.8) vs 10.8 (2.6), 20% lower (p. 132; Table 4). Editors' calculation from Table 4: 32% lower overall; unadjusted difference 4.9 ng/ml (95% CI 1.7 to 8.1, Welch t test); standardized difference about 0.82 (95% CI 0.28 to 1.35) with the pooled SD, or 0.62 with the control SD (the two SDs differ more than twofold); men alone 2.6 ng/ml (-0.6 to 5.8), p about .10; women alone 8.6 (2.2 to 15.0), p about .01. HVA: 27.4 (21.3; range 8.1 to 117.9) vs 19.4 (7.8) ng/ml; group F(1, 52) = 6.9, p = .01, interaction F(1, 52) = 4.3, p = .04; lower only in MDMA women vs control women, 18.7 (7.0) vs 34.8 (29.9) (pp. 132-133); editors' calculation, unadjusted Welch tests: p about .07 overall and about .11 in women. MHPG 8.5 vs 8.5, no effects (p. 133). Height and 5-HIAA: r = -.42 (p = .03) in controls and r = .18 (p = .34) in the MDMA group (p. 132); editors' calculation: the two correlations differ (Fisher z = 2.27, p about .02). 5-HIAA and number of MDMA exposures r = -0.2, p = .33; not significantly correlated with duration or frequency of use or time since last use, coefficients not given (p. 132). Season: no effect (F(3, 50) = .89, p = .45). Prolactin: no drug effects on peak change or area under the curve (p. 133; Table 5). Pain: gender effects only are reported (p. 134; Table 6). Personality: MPQ control scale higher (less impulsive) in the MDMA group, F(1, 52) = 9.21, p = .004; Buss-Durkee indirect hostility lower, F(1, 52) = 7.4, p = .009, the difference coming from control women; EPQ impulsivity and sociability no differences (p. 134).
analysis.covariates: Age and height for CSF metabolites; age, basal prolactin and plasma tryptophan for prolactin; age and education for personality (Methods, p. 132; the MPQ paragraph names age only, p. 134). Other drug use, education (for CSF), diet before admission, smoking and alcohol were not adjusted for.
analysis.selective_reporting: The abstract reports lower impulsivity (p = .004) from the MPQ control scale but not that the EPQ impulsivity subscale showed no difference (p. 134). Correlations between CSF 5-HIAA and personality scales are given as p values only, without coefficients (p. 134). For pain endurance and tolerance only gender effects are reported, although Table 6 shows lower values in MDMA men than in control men (p. 134). The arrival drug-screen results are not reported.
analysis.power: Not reported. With 30 and 28 participants and the wide spread of control values, the interval for the 5-HIAA difference is wide: about 11% to 53% below the control mean (editors' calculation from the Welch interval).

interpretation_gap.results_show: Lumbar CSF 5-HIAA was about a third lower in 30 self-referred people who had used MDMA many times than in 28 controls. The difference was clear in women (12 vs 11) and is not marked as significant in men; it was unrelated to the number of occasions, duration, frequency or recency of use. HVA was lower only in women; prolactin and pain responses did not differ; and the MDMA group scored as less impulsive and less hostile, the opposite of what low CSF 5-HIAA goes with in the clinical groups the authors cite.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract and the summary present the CSF finding as suggesting that serotonin neurotoxicity may be a complication of MDMA use, and the summary says MDMA neurotoxicity "may generalize to humans" (p. 136); the title states serotonin neurotoxicity as the subject of the finding. The Discussion describes the controls as matched for education and other drug use (p. 135), which Tables 1 and 3 contradict, and sets aside other drugs and premorbid factors by argument, not analysis (p. 136). The neurotoxicity reading rests on the similarity to CSF decrements in MDMA-treated monkeys (pp. 135-136); the authors also write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from CSF data alone (p. 135). The personality differences, opposite to the expected direction, are read post hoc as support for serotonin modulating these traits (abstract; pp. 135-136).

timeline.event: Peroutka and colleagues: CSF monoamine metabolites in people who used MDMA recreationally; no reduction in 5-HIAA (as described in this paper's introduction, p. 130, which notes the setting was not controlled).
Ricaurte and colleagues: preliminary report of reduced CSF 5-HIAA in people previously exposed to MDMA (as described, p. 130; setting not controlled).
This study: controlled inpatient comparison, 30 vs 28.

Ung et al. cite this study, with a 1999 study from the same group (not read), for reduced CSF 5-HIAA as support for possible serotonin neurotoxicity, and also cite it as indirect human evidence of dopamine-system damage (pp. 274, 281), although the HVA difference was confined to women.

replication.where_it_stands: Before this study one uncontrolled CSF study had found lower 5-HIAA and one had not (as described on p. 130). Later CSF studies are not among the papers read in this batch; a 2026 review cites this study and a 1999 study by the same group for reduced CSF 5-HIAA (Ung et al., 2026, p. 281; the 1999 study not read). Independent replication of the controlled CSF finding is not documented in the papers read here. The study measured no memory or thinking outcome, so it cannot be cited on the cognition claims.

funding.funder: US Public Health Service research grant R01DA05938 from the National Institute on Drug Abuse, and General Clinical Research Center grant 5M01RR02719 (Acknowledgments, p. 136).
funding.declared_conflicts: No conflict-of-interest statement in the article.
funding.affiliations_note: National Institute of Mental Health (Bethesda), Johns Hopkins Medical Institutions (Baltimore) and Concordia University (Montreal). The neurotoxicity reading leans on monkey studies by the senior author (cited on pp. 130 and 135-136), and the MDMA group was recruited through contact with him about MDMA research (p. 130). Recorded as a flag for closer reading, not as a reason to discount the results.

what_would_settle_it: A prospective study measuring CSF 5-HIAA and a direct marker of serotonin nerve terminals (for example serotonin transporter imaging) before and after people begin regular MDMA use, against people who use the same other drugs but not MDMA, with exposure confirmed by hair analysis, testing of memory and thinking, and a dose-response analysis across a wide range of use.

domains.note: Other drug use far more common in the MDMA group (cocaine, hallucinogens, benzodiazepines, sedative-hypnotics, amphetamines) and not adjusted for; less education in MDMA men; diet before admission, smoking and alcohol not reported; premorbid serotonin function unknown.
Self-reported number of occasions and amounts, tablet content unknown, usual amount misprinted; arrival drug screens not reported.
Self-referred MDMA group in contact with an MDMA research programme, described by the authors as often strong advocates of the drug; some controls referred by them.
Time since last use ranged from 2 weeks to 2 years with abstinence verified only on arrival (results not shown); 5-HIAA was not related to time since last use.
CSF data complete for 58; prolactin data missing for 7 of 58 without explanation.

For CSF 5-HIAA: standardized diet, time of day and bed rest, assays blind to group, low assay variation. The personality outcomes would be some concerns (self-report by people the authors describe as advocates).

Several analysis models (one-way, group x gender, group x season); the abstract selects the MPQ control scale over the null EPQ impulsivity result; personality correlations reported without coefficients.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: The CSF measurement itself is careful (inpatient stay, low-monoamine diet, fixed time of sampling, blind assays), but the comparison is confounded by much heavier use of other drugs in a self-selected MDMA group, with no adjustment and no measure before use; the difference rests mainly on women, and 5-HIAA showed no relation to any measure of MDMA use. The study may be cited for lower lumbar CSF 5-HIAA in this group under controlled conditions. It may not be cited as showing that MDMA damages serotonin neurons, that the deficit is dose-related, or that MDMA affects memory or thinking.

key_findings.finding: Lumbar CSF 5-HIAA was 10.3 (SD 3.1) ng/ml in 30 people who had used MDMA at least 25 times vs 15.2 (7.9; range 4.8 to 37.3) in 28 controls; ANCOVA with age and height F(1, 54) = 11.6, p = .001; group x gender ANCOVA group F(1, 52) = 14.9, p < .001. Editors' calculation: about 32% lower; unadjusted difference 4.9 ng/ml (95% CI 1.7 to 8.1).
key_findings.locator: Results › CSF Monoamine Metabolites › 5-HIAA, 1st paragraph (p. 132); Table 4 (p. 133)

key_findings.finding: The difference depended on sex (group x gender F(1, 52) = 5.1, p < .03): 46% lower in women (10.1 vs 18.7 ng/ml; 12 vs 11), marked significant, and 20% lower in men (10.8 vs 13.4; 18 vs 17), not marked significant in Table 4. Control women had higher 5-HIAA than control men.
key_findings.locator: Results › 5-HIAA, 1st paragraph (p. 132); Table 4 and its footnotes (p. 133)
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, unadjusted Welch tests: men 2.6 ng/ml (95% CI -0.6 to 5.8), p about .10; women 8.6 (2.2 to 15.0), p about .01. The authors explain the sex difference by greater exposure in women rather than greater susceptibility: women reported about 115 occasions against 85 for men and weighed less while reporting the same amount per occasion (p. 135). That explanation sits against the absence of any relation between 5-HIAA and the number of exposures within the group (r = -0.2, p = .33).

key_findings.finding: CSF 5-HIAA was not significantly related to the number of MDMA exposures (r = -0.2, p = .33), duration or frequency of use, or time since last use (coefficients not given).

Height correlated negatively with CSF 5-HIAA in controls (r = -.42, p = .03) but not in the MDMA group (r = .18, p = .34); the authors read the missing gradient as a sign that MDMA damages ascending more than descending serotonin projections.
key_findings.note: No test of the difference between the two correlations is reported; editors' calculation, Fisher z = 2.27, p about .02.

key_findings.finding: Season had no effect on CSF 5-HIAA and no interaction with group (F(3, 50) = .89, p = .45).

CSF HVA (a dopamine metabolite): 27.4 (21.3; range 8.1 to 117.9) in controls vs 19.4 (7.8) ng/ml; group F(1, 52) = 6.9, p = .01, group x gender F(1, 52) = 4.3, p = .04; lower only in MDMA women than control women (18.7 vs 34.8, control SD 29.9), not in men (22.1 vs 24.6). MHPG did not differ (8.5 vs 8.5).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, unadjusted Welch tests: p about .07 overall and about .11 in women; the control-women SD of 29.9 suggests one or more very high values.

key_findings.finding: Prolactin before and after intravenous L-tryptophan showed gender effects but no significant drug effects on peak change or area under the curve.
key_findings.note: Table 5 shows the MDMA groups numerically above the control groups on the post-tryptophan peak (women 33.8 vs 30.3, men 14.8 vs 13.4), so the neuroendocrine result is not only non-significant but in the opposite direction to the blunting reported in 1988 and set aside here.

key_findings.finding: The authors explain the normal prolactin response by possible recovery of serotonin axons to the hypothalamus in the months after exposure, citing monkey work, and note that participants had last used MDMA about 18 weeks earlier, some up to 2 years; they offer as an alternative that the serotonin deficit behind the lower 5-HIAA may be too small or wrongly placed to produce a neuroendocrine effect.
key_findings.note: Second-hand for the monkey evidence (not read). This is the only reversibility argument in the paper and is relevant to the tolerance and recovery questions (METHODS §8, section 5).

key_findings.finding: Ischaemic pain: gender effects on sensitivity (F(1, 54) = 5.7, p = .02) and tolerance (F(1, 54) = 4.9, p = .03); no effect of group on sensitivity; no significant effects of group or gender on endurance.
key_findings.locator: Results › Pain Measures, 1st to 3rd paragraphs; Table 6

key_findings.finding: Personality: the MDMA group scored higher on the MPQ control scale (less impulsive; F(1, 52) = 9.21, p = .004) and lower on Buss-Durkee indirect hostility (F(1, 52) = 7.4, p = .009; both MDMA subgroups lower than control women, neither different from control men); no differences on the EPQ impulsivity and sociability subscales.
key_findings.locator: Results › Personality Measures (MPQ; BDHI; EPQ paragraphs)

key_findings.finding: Lifetime use of other drug classes, MDMA group (30) vs controls (28): cocaine 24 (80%) vs 8 (29%); LSD and other hallucinogens 26 (87%) vs 9 (32%); benzodiazepines 18 (60%) vs 6 (21%); sedative-hypnotics 10 (33%) vs 1 (4%); non-MDMA amphetamines 13 (43%) vs 4 (14%); opiates 16 (53%) vs 9 (32%); cannabis 28 (93%) vs 22 (printed 73%).
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation, Fisher exact tests: cocaine and hallucinogens p < .001, benzodiazepines p about .004, sedative-hypnotics p about .006, amphetamines p about .02; cannabis p about .14.

key_findings.finding: MDMA use as self-reported: 94.4 (SD 90.6) occasions (range 25 to 300) over 4.98 (2.96) years, 4.16 (4.79) times a month; last use 17.9 (24.7) weeks before admission (range 2 to 104).

Men in the MDMA group had less education than control men (14.8 vs 17.2 years, marked significant; group x gender interaction F(1, 53) = 4.4, p = .04); the age difference (32.3 vs 27.8 years) was not significant (F(1, 54) = 2.31, p = .13).

The authors write that the nature of the alteration is difficult to establish from CSF data alone and base the neurotoxicity reading on similar CSF 5-HIAA decrements in MDMA-treated monkeys with known serotonin deficits; they describe the controls as matched for age, height, weight, gender, education and other drug use.

The authors consider and set aside three alternatives: a premorbid condition (screening for psychiatric disorders), other drugs (controls also used them, to a lesser extent) and changes in serotonin turnover unrelated to toxicity (similar CSF findings in monkeys); they also raise biased questionnaire answers by people who were often strong advocates of MDMA.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 prints the usual amount as 170 (SD .82) mg with a range of 0.5 to 4, and a footnote saying it was estimated from the number of capsules or tablets taken; a mean of 170 cannot lie outside a range of 0.5 to 4, and the unit appears to be tablets or capsules, not mg. The Discussion refers to a usual amount of one tablet or capsule (p. 135).
reporting_issues.consequence: The sample's usual amount per occasion cannot be stated from the paper.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 3 gives cannabis use in controls as 22 (73%); 22 of 28 is 79%, and 73% matches no whole number out of 28.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either the count or the percentage is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The Discussion describes the controls as matched for education and other drug use (p. 135), but Table 1 marks lower education in MDMA men (14.8 vs 17.2 years) and Table 3 shows more lifetime use of most other drug classes in the MDMA group (p. 131).
reporting_issues.consequence: The main finding is presented as free of confounders that the paper's own tables show were not matched; no analysis adjusts for them.

reporting_issues.issue: The alienation interaction is printed as F(1, 52) = 4.4, p = .004; an F of 4.4 on 1 and 52 degrees of freedom gives p of about .04 (editors' calculation).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; either the F or the p value is misprinted.

reporting_issues.issue: The text reports a significant overall group effect on HVA (F(1, 52) = 6.9, p = .01), but Table 4 does not mark the overall HVA difference; the women's difference rests on a control-women SD of 29.9 with control values up to 117.9 ng/ml, and unequal-variance tests are not significant (editors' calculation, p about .07 overall and .11 in women).
reporting_issues.consequence: The HVA finding, used later as indirect evidence of dopamine-system damage (Ung et al., 2026, p. 274), is fragile.

reporting_issues.issue: The group x season ANCOVA is reported with F(3, 50); a 2 x 4 design with two covariates in 58 people leaves 48 error degrees of freedom (editors' arithmetic).
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the model fitted may differ from the one described.

reporting_issues.issue: The prolactin analysis includes 51 of 58 participants (control women 7 of 11) without explanation.
reporting_issues.consequence: Missing data in the functional measure that was expected to show a deficit; the null result is less informative for women.

reporting_issues.issue: Correlations between CSF 5-HIAA and personality scales are reported as p values only, without coefficients; the Discussion then speaks of a negative correlation between CSF 5-HIAA and control, which was not significant (p = .06 in women).
reporting_issues.consequence: The strength of these relations cannot be judged, and a non-significant result is treated as a finding.

reporting_issues.issue: Methods state that personality measures were analysed with age and education as covariates (p. 132); the MPQ paragraph names age only (p. 134). The reported degrees of freedom (52) fit two covariates.
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor inconsistency in the description of the model.

reporting_issues.issue: For pain endurance and tolerance the text reports gender effects only, but Table 6 shows MDMA men below control men on both (endurance 9.9 vs 12.2; tolerance 114 vs 157); group and interaction statistics for these measures are not given.
reporting_issues.consequence: The abstract's statement that the groups resembled each other in their response to ischaemic pain may not hold for men.

disagreements.first_pass: Editors' calculation, unadjusted Welch tests: men 2.6 ng/ml (95% CI -0.6 to 5.8), p about .10; women 8.6 (2.2 to 15.0), p about .01.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): the paper's own explanation of the sex difference (p. 135) is greater exposure in women (about 115 occasions against 85, at lower body weight), which sits awkwardly beside the absence of a relation with the number of exposures.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 135 (Discussion, 3rd paragraph): both statements are there, in those numbers. Added to the note, with the tension against r = -0.2 stated, because any dose-response reading of this study turns on it.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): Table 5 shows MDMA women and men numerically above their control groups on the prolactin peak, so the result is not merely null.
disagreements.resolution: Checked against Table 5 (p. 133): 33.8 against 30.3 in women and 14.8 against 13.4 in men. Added as a note, because the card's prolactin finding is otherwise read as a bare null.

disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): the authors explain the normal prolactin response by possible recovery of hypothalamic serotonin axons in the months after exposure (p. 135), evidence the encyclopedia will need for reversibility and tolerance.
disagreements.resolution: Checked at p. 135 (Discussion, 4th paragraph): the recovery argument, the 18-week average and the up-to-2-year range are there, with an alternative explanation offered. Added as a key finding, with the alternative recorded so the argument is not read as a finding.

disagreements.first_pass: Before this study one uncontrolled CSF study had found lower 5-HIAA and one had not (as described on p. 130). Later CSF studies are not among the papers read in this batch; a 2026 review cites this study and a 1999 study by the same group for reduced CSF 5-HIAA (Ung et al., 2026, p. 281; the 1999 study not read). Independent replication of the controlled CSF finding is not documented in the papers read here.
disagreements.reviewer: Missed (AI reader 31): the card says under cannot_establish that no cognition was measured, but the replication field discusses only CSF studies.
disagreements.resolution: Added one sentence. The point is already in cannot_establish; repeating it here is a convenience for anyone reading the field, not a new finding.
